UPHYS:001.title: Displacement is endpoint minus start
UPHYS:001.objective: Compute a two-dimensional displacement, its magnitude, and its signed direction without confusing position with distance traveled.
UPHYS:001.statement: In an Earth-fixed frame, take $+x$ east and $+y$ north. A cart moves from $\mathbf r_i=(-2.0\,\mathbf e_x+1.0\,\mathbf e_y)\,\mathrm m$ to $\mathbf r_f=(4.0\,\mathbf e_x-3.0\,\mathbf e_y)\,\mathrm m$. Find $\Delta\mathbf r$, its magnitude, and its direction measured counterclockwise from $+x$. State what changes if the trip is reversed.
permittedResults: $\Delta\mathbf r=\mathbf r_f-\mathbf r_i$.
The Pythagorean theorem and the two-argument arctangent.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Subtract initial components from final components in the stated frame. Next: Use $|\Delta\mathbf r|=\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}$ and preserve the quadrant. Finally: Reverse the vector, not its magnitude, for the return trip.

Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Reverse the vector, not its magnitude, for the return trip.

commonErrors.description: Adds the endpoint coordinates and reports $(2,-2)\,\mathrm m$ as the displacement.
commonErrors.consequence: Displacement is a difference of positions; the proposed vector depends on the arbitrary coordinate origin.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\tan^{-1}(|-4/6|)$ and reports a first-quadrant direction.
commonErrors.consequence: Discarding component signs puts the vector in the wrong quadrant.

Use $|\Delta\mathbf r|=\sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}$ and preserve the quadrant.

UPHYS:001.canonicalSolution:
Component subtraction gives $\Delta\mathbf r=(6.0\,\mathbf e_x-4.0\,\mathbf e_y)\,\mathrm m$. Thus $|\Delta\mathbf r|=\sqrt{52}\,\mathrm m=2\sqrt{13}\,\mathrm m\approx7.21\,\mathrm m$, and $\operatorname{atan2}(-4,6)\approx-33.7^\circ$ (equivalently $326.3^\circ$ counterclockwise from $+x$). Reversing the trip gives $-\Delta\mathbf r$ with the same $7.21\,\mathrm m$ magnitude. The component squares sum to $52\,\mathrm{m^2}$, which checks both units and magnitude.

UPHYS:049.objective: Derive every translation, Euler, Coriolis, centripetal, and relative term in rotating-frame kinematics and apply them consistently.
UPHYS:049.statement: A frame with origin $O'$ translates with inertial acceleration $\mathbf A_O$ and rotates with angular velocity $\boldsymbol\Omega(t)$. A particle has rotating-frame position $\mathbf r$, relative velocity $\mathbf v_{rel}$, and relative acceleration $\mathbf a_{rel}$. Derive its inertial velocity and acceleration. Then take a fixed origin, constant $\boldsymbol\Omega=2.00\,\mathbf e_z\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and at one instant $\mathbf r=0.500\,\mathbf e_x\,\mathrm m$, $\mathbf v_{rel}=0.300\,\mathbf e_x\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\mathbf a_{rel}=\mathbf0$. Find the inertial velocity and acceleration.
permittedResults: For any vector, $(d\mathbf q/dt)_I=(d\mathbf q/dt)_R+\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf q$.
The origin translation and rotating relative position add to inertial position.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Differentiate $\mathbf r_P=\mathbf R_O+\mathbf r$ once using the rotating-vector derivative rule. Next: Differentiate again, applying the same rule separately to $\mathbf v_{rel}$ and $\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r$. Finally: Evaluate each surviving cross product and check the $\boldsymbol\Omega\to0$ limit.

milestones.criterion: Chooses and states the correct kinematic setup: Differentiate $\mathbf r_P=\mathbf R_O+\mathbf r$ once using the rotating-vector derivative rule.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Differentiate again, applying the same rule separately to $\mathbf v_{rel}$ and $\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r$.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Evaluate each surviving cross product and check the $\boldsymbol\Omega\to0$ limit.

commonErrors.description: Includes only one $\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v_{rel}$ term.
commonErrors.consequence: The product appears from differentiating both relative velocity and the rotating-position contribution, producing the factor two.

commonErrors.description: Uses $+\Omega^2\mathbf r$ for the centripetal term.
commonErrors.consequence: For $\mathbf r\perp\boldsymbol\Omega$, the double cross product is $-\Omega^2\mathbf r$, directed inward.

hintTree.content: Differentiate $\mathbf r_P=\mathbf R_O+\mathbf r$ once using the rotating-vector derivative rule.
Differentiate again, applying the same rule separately to $\mathbf v_{rel}$ and $\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r$.
Evaluate each surviving cross product and check the $\boldsymbol\Omega\to0$ limit.

UPHYS:049.canonicalSolution:
The inertial velocity is $\mathbf v_I=\mathbf V_O+\mathbf v_{rel}+\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r$. A second differentiation gives $\mathbf a_I=\mathbf A_O+\mathbf a_{rel}+2\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf v_{rel}+\dot{\boldsymbol\Omega}\times\mathbf r+\boldsymbol\Omega\times(\boldsymbol\Omega\times\mathbf r)$. For the data, $\mathbf v_I=(0.300\,\mathbf e_x+1.00\,\mathbf e_y)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The centripetal term is $-2.00\,\mathbf e_x\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and the Coriolis term is $1.20\,\mathbf e_y\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, so $\mathbf a_I=(-2.00\,\mathbf e_x+1.20\,\mathbf e_y)\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. When $\boldsymbol\Omega\to0$, only origin and relative terms remain.

UPHYS:050.title: Curvature and torsion of a helical trajectory
UPHYS:050.objective: Derive three-dimensional curvature and torsion directly from a time-parametric helix and verify circle and straight-line limits.
UPHYS:050.statement: A particle follows $\mathbf r(t)=(R\cos\omega t,R\sin\omega t,ct)$, where $R>0$, $\omega>0$, and constant $c$ has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Derive its speed, curvature $\kappa=|\mathbf v\times\mathbf a|/|\mathbf v|^3$, and torsion $\tau=[(\mathbf v\times\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf j]/|\mathbf v\times\mathbf a|^2$, with $\mathbf j=d\mathbf a/dt$. Evaluate them for $R=2.00\,\mathrm m$, $\omega=3.00\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $c=4.00\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
permittedResults: The stated curvature and torsion formulas for a regular parameterized curve.
Standard cross and dot products in a fixed orthonormal basis.

acceptableStrategies.description: First: Differentiate the helix three times and simplify the constant speed first. Next: Compute $\mathbf v\times\mathbf a$ before taking its magnitude and dotting with jerk. Finally: Simplify symbolically, then evaluate and test $c\to0$ and $R\to0$ limits.

milestones.criterion: Chooses and states the correct kinematic setup: Differentiate the helix three times and simplify the constant speed first.
Executes the central calculation or derivation correctly: Compute $\mathbf v\times\mathbf a$ before taking its magnitude and dotting with jerk.
Reports and checks the physical conclusion: Simplify symbolically, then evaluate and test $c\to0$ and $R\to0$ limits.

commonErrors.description: Uses acceleration magnitude divided by speed squared as curvature without removing tangential effects or checking the cross product.
commonErrors.consequence: That shortcut is not generally valid and obscures the three-dimensional geometry.

commonErrors.description: Treats torsion as dimensionless because it measures twisting.
commonErrors.consequence: The formula has units of inverse length, as does curvature.

hintTree.content: Differentiate the helix three times and simplify the constant speed first.
Compute $\mathbf v\times\mathbf a$ before taking its magnitude and dotting with jerk.
Simplify symbolically, then evaluate and test $c\to0$ and $R\to0$ limits.

UPHYS:050.canonicalSolution:
$|\mathbf v|=\sqrt{R^2\omega^2+c^2}$. Direct cross-product simplification gives $\kappa=R\omega^2/(R^2\omega^2+c^2)$ and $\tau=c\omega/(R^2\omega^2+c^2)$. For the data, speed is $\sqrt{52}\approx7.21\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\kappa=18/52=9/26\approx0.346\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, and $\tau=12/52=3/13\approx0.231\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. When $c\to0$, $\kappa\to1/R$ and $\tau\to0$, the circle result. As $R\to0$ with $c\ne0$, $\kappa\to0$ but the simplified torsion tends to $\omega/c$; at exactly $R=0$, $\mathbf v\times\mathbf a=\mathbf0$ and Frenet torsion is undefined. This nonuniform limit correctly flags degeneration to a straight line rather than licensing the torsion formula at $R=0$.

[[PROOFBOUND_LEAN4_DRAFT_END]]

For the data, speed is $\sqrt{52}\approx7.21\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\kappa=18/52=9/26\approx0.346\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, and $\tau=12/52=3/13\approx0.231\,\mathrm{m^{-1}}$. When $c\to0$, $\kappa\to1/R$ and $\tau\to0$, the circle result. UPHYS:287.objective: Model, solve, and audit orbit after instantaneous central mass loss using the appropriate balance law and an independent physical check.

System and conventions: Use an inertial frame with the stated origin and radial sign convention; use Newtonian gravity, point or spherical bodies as stated, and SI units. The radial energy uses $U_{\mathrm{eff}}=L^2/(2\mu r^2)-GMm/r$. Its stationary radius is $r_c=L^2/(G M m\mu)=L^2/[G\mu^2(M+m)]$. At $r_c$, $U_{\mathrm{eff}}''=GMm/r_c^3>0$, so the orbit is radially stable, and $n^2=G(M+m)/r_c^3$. The simple tidal-survival condition is $r_c>R_m(2M/m)^{1/3}$; material structure can change the order-one coefficient. Check: In the test-mass limit, the frequency becomes $GM/r_c^3$ and the circular-radius formula reduces to the fixed-primary result.
